questions.scenario: A legacy wallet stores passwords as SHA-256(salt + password). The team argues this is fine because each password has its own salt.
questions.question: Why is this still weak, and what should replace it?
options: It should use MD5, which is faster to compute
It should be replaced with AES encryption so passwords can be recovered
SHA-256 is designed to be fast, so attackers can try billions of guesses per second; use a slow, memory-hard algorithm such as Argon2id (or BCrypt)
Salts make SHA-256 unbreakable, so nothing needs to change
questions.explanation: Salting stops precomputed tables but not fast brute force. Password hashes must be deliberately slow and, ideally, memory-hard.

questions.scenario: You are moving users from BCrypt to Argon2id without forcing everyone to reset their password.
questions.question: Which approach works with Spring Security?
options: Ask users to email their passwords to support
Use a DelegatingPasswordEncoder that recognises both {bcrypt} and Argon2 hashes, and re-hash with Argon2id when a user logs in successfully
Store both hashes and compare either
Decrypt the BCrypt hashes and re-hash them with Argon2id in a batch job
questions.explanation: Hashes cannot be reversed, so upgrades happen at login when the plain password is briefly available. The prefix in the stored value tells the delegating encoder which algorithm to use.

questions.scenario: A developer accidentally pushed a live payment-gateway secret key to a private GitHub repository and removed it in the next commit an hour later.
questions.question: What is the first thing to do?
options: Rewrite Git history and consider the incident closed
Nothing: the repository is private and the key was removed
Make the repository public so everyone can see it was removed
Revoke and rotate the key at the gateway immediately, then check its usage logs
questions.explanation: Once pushed, a secret must be treated as compromised: history, clones, CI logs and integrations may have copied it. Rotation removes its value; history clean-up is secondary.

questions.scenario: A new CVE with CVSS 9.8 is announced for a logging library. Your manager asks within the hour which of your 40 services are affected.
questions.question: What lets you answer quickly?
options: Searching each repository's pom.xml for the library name
Waiting for Dependabot to open pull requests
Asking each team lead
An SBOM (for example CycloneDX) generated for every build, listing all direct and transitive dependencies and versions
questions.explanation: Most vulnerable libraries arrive transitively and do not appear in pom.xml. A stored SBOM per build lets you query exact versions across services in minutes.

questions.scenario: You are designing how a Spring Boot service on AWS gets its database password in production.
questions.question: Which practices are appropriate? (Choose two.)
options: Use a dedicated database user for this service with only the privileges it needs, and rotate the password regularly
Commit it to application-prod.yml in a private repository
Load it from AWS Secrets Manager at startup, with an IAM role allowing access only to this service's secret
Bake the password into the Docker image as an environment variable
questions.explanation: Secrets belong in a managed store with least-privilege access and rotation. Anything in an image or a repository spreads to every copy and is hard to rotate.

questions.scenario: OWASP Dependency-Check flags a CVE in a library your service uses. The vulnerable function is in a module you do not call, and no fixed version exists yet.
questions.question: What is the professional response?
options: Remove the library immediately even if the service stops working
Disable the scanner for the whole project
Document the analysis and add a suppression with a reason and an expiry date, then upgrade as soon as a fix is released
Suppress it permanently without comment
questions.explanation: Triage means understanding reachability and recording the decision. An expiry forces a re-check, and the upgrade happens when possible.

questions.scenario: A KYC service must store customers' BVNs and also find a customer by BVN.
questions.question: Which design protects the data while keeping lookups possible?
options: Store the BVN in plain text with a unique index
Encrypt it with AES-ECB using a key in application.yml
Encrypt the BVN with AES-GCM under a KMS-managed key, and store a separate keyed hash (HMAC) of the BVN for lookups
Store only an unsalted SHA-256 of the BVN and nothing else
questions.explanation: Authenticated encryption with managed keys protects the value; a keyed hash allows equality lookups without decrypting everything. An unsalted plain hash of an 11-digit number is easy to brute-force, and ECB with a key in config is not protection.
